races.note: Charter amendment: ranked-choice voting for Longmont mayor and city council from November 2029, once the Secretary of State certifies equipment and rules. Yes = adopt RCV.

assessment.threshold: Simple majority of votes cast on the question
assessment.summary: Both data sources point to about 60% Yes, roughly an 88% chance of passing. Across 10 local RCV votes, a city as Democratic as Longmont (Harris 70% of the two-party vote in its Boulder County precincts) would be expected to give about 60%. Longmont also voted on statewide RCV in 2024: Prop 131 got 48.8% Yes there, almost exactly what it got in Boulder (48.1%) and Broomfield (48.2%). Those two cities then passed their own RCV measures with 78% and 52%. Adjusted to Longmont’s partisanship, those votes average about 61%.
for: Council referred it 6-1. Mayor Susie Hidalgo-Fahring, Councilmember Alex Kalkhofer, State Sen. Katie Wallace and State Rep. Karen McCormick support it
League of Women Voters of Boulder County supports RCV, and a ‘Ranked Choice Voting for Longmont’ campaign is active
No tax increase, modest stated cost, and delayed to 2029 behind state certification
Nearby Boulder already uses RCV for mayor, so the system is familiar in the county
against: The city’s con summary argues RCV is more complex, can ‘exhaust’ ballots, and should have come from a citizen petition, not the council
Colorado voters rejected statewide RCV (Prop 131) in 2024
Longmont is more politically mixed than Boulder (it extends into Weld County)
assessment.finance: Longmont committees report through a city dashboard that this site can’t read automatically, so spending wasn’t checked. Local reporting names no opposition committee.

model.anchor_label: Boulder and Broomfield RCV votes, adjusted to Longmont
model.anchor_detail: On 2024’s statewide Prop 131, Longmont (48.8% Yes), Boulder city (48.1%) and Broomfield (48.2%) voted almost identically. Their own city RCV votes were 78.1% and 51.9%; moved to Longmont’s partisanship that’s 66.3% and 55.5%.

assessment.turnout: Through Oct. 29 (5 days out), Longmont had returned 24,460 ballots, 26% more than at the same point in 2022. Boulder County’s early electorate is D+37.0 by registration, the same as in 2022 (D+36.8), so the turnout mix doesn’t move the estimate.

races.note: Charter amendment: realigns council election cycles so all at-large seats are elected together and all ward seats together (two seats get one-time two-year terms). Takes effect only if 3C passes. Yes = realign.

assessment.threshold: Simple majority of votes cast on the question; has no effect unless 3C also passes
assessment.summary: This rides on 3C and has no voting history of its own to model. The estimate takes 3C’s number and subtracts 4 points. That drop-off is an assumption: companion process measures usually trail the headline measure, but there’s no good dataset to measure by how much. The range is widened to reflect that. It has no effect unless 3C passes. Its 75% chance is the chance of getting a majority. Since it only matters if 3C also passes, and the two votes will move together, the chance it actually takes effect is about 70%.
for: Same endorsers and campaign as 3C, which pitches them as a pair
Lets the at-large race use a multi-winner ranked method (single transferable vote), which supporters argue gives fairer representation
against: The city’s con summary calls it unnecessary and warns of ‘lame duck’ two-year terms
Process changes with no clear everyday payoff tend to underperform the headline measure they travel with
Voters who oppose 3C will almost all vote No here too
assessment.finance: Same as 3C: not checked; no opposition committee reported.
